strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: evaluating episodic memory utilization for personalized assistance in embodied agents is genuinely underexplored, and the paper convincingly argues why existing single-turn instruction-following benchmarks miss this challenge.

The two-stage evaluation design (Memory Acquisition vs. Memory Utilization) is a clean experimental methodology: by holding the scene S and goal g fixed while varying only the instruction I, the framework isolates memory-based goal interpretation from general task-execution capability. The validation experiment (Figure 3) showing near-zero success without memory confirms the design actually measures memory utilization.

Broad and reasonably thorough evaluation: six LLMs spanning proprietary and open-source families, multiple metrics (PC, SR, planning cycles, sim steps), and a good set of analyses (knowledge-type breakdown, top-k retrieval degradation, gold vs. retrieved memory quality, trajectory vs. instruction-only memory, ambiguous references).

The finding that agents rely on commonsense knowledge over personalized memory even when relevant memory is available (C.1/D.1 error pattern) and that action trajectories contain essential procedural cues (Table 2) are actionable insights for future memory system design.
Good supporting material: dataset statistics, generation prompts, skill library descriptions, licensing, and limitations are documented, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Circularity in data generation and quality control: personalized instructions are generated by GPT-4o, and episodes where GPT-4o fails five consecutive attempts are filtered out (13.4% of data removed). This biases the benchmark toward tasks solvable by the very model being evaluated, potentially understating difficulty and confounding cross-model comparisons. Golden trajectories are also GPT-4o-generated.

Limited scale and statistical power: only 438 episodes over 12 scenes, with just 36 joint-memory episodes (12 per pair type). Reported success-rate differences (e.g., Llama-3.1-70b SR of 8.3% in Table 1) are based on very few episodes, yet no confidence intervals or significance tests are provided for the main results, making several headline claims (e.g., the 30.5% GPT-4o drop) statistically fragile.

The retrieval setup artificially guarantees the correct memory is always included in the top-5 (by random replacement if not retrieved). This weakens the realism of the retrieval analysis and makes the top-k degradation findings mostly about in-context distraction rather than end-to-end memory system performance.

The paper is purely evaluative: no memory-augmented methods (e.g., summarization, structured memory, reflection-based recall) are compared against the naive retrieval baseline, limiting the benchmark's demonstrated usefulness for driving progress and leaving the practical implications of the identified failure modes untested.

Several findings are fairly expected (irrelevant memories distract agents; multi-memory integration is harder than single-memory; user patterns are harder than object semantics), so the conceptual novelty beyond the two-stage design is moderate.

Ecological validity concerns acknowledged but significant: oracle perception/motor skills, text-only observations, and a simulator setting mean the results may not transfer to visually grounded agents, and the ambiguous-instruction extension (Section 6.2) uses only 30 episodes authored by the authors themselves.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: evaluating whether LLM-powered embodied agents can leverage episodic memory containing personalized knowledge (object semantics, user patterns) for object rearrangement tasks.

The two-stage evaluation design (Memory Acquisition vs. Memory Utilization) with shared scene S and goal g is a reasonable attempt to isolate instruction interpretation / memory utilization from other confounds, and Section 4.4 provides a sanity validation that the utilization-stage instructions are indeed unsolvable without memory.

Decent breadth of evaluation: six LLMs spanning open-source and proprietary families, plus several analyses (knowledge-type breakdown, top-k retrieval sensitivity, memory-trajectory ablation, memory quality via gold trajectories, ambiguous reference probe) and a qualitative error taxonomy.
The writing is clear and the framework components (POMDP formulation, task construction, metrics from PartNR) are described in enough detail to understand the pipeline.
weaknesses: A serious methodological flaw: the retrieval setup 'ensures the corresponding memory is included in the retrieved results by randomly replacing one memory if the correct one is not initially retrieved.' This oracle intervention means the benchmark does not actually measure retrieval, yet the authors draw conclusions about 'irrelevant memories acting as distractors' and about memory utilization broadly. Results with a realistic retrieval setup (no oracle patching) are not reported.

The headline claim of a '30.5% performance drop' for GPT-4o is based on the joint-memory setting, which contains only 36 episodes (12 pairs per type). Success rates such as 8.3% or 5.6% imply denominators far too small for the reported precision, and no confidence intervals or variance estimates are given for the utilization-stage results.

The dataset is heavily GPT-4o-generated (instructions, personalized knowledge, captions), and quality control filters out any episode where GPT-4o fails five consecutive attempts. This biases the benchmark toward phenomena GPT-4o can handle, potentially inflating all models' scores and undermining the claim that the benchmark captures real personalization difficulty.

The central measurement conflates memory utilization with instruction-understanding difficulty: the utilization-stage instructions are also shorter, more implicit, and differently phrased than acquisition-stage instructions, so part of the reported drop may be attributable to instruction ambiguity rather than failure to use episodic memory. No control experiment (e.g., providing the personalized knowledge directly in-context) cleanly separates these factors.

No memory-method baselines: the paper evaluates only a vanilla ReAct agent with embedding-based retrieval. It does not compare against any existing memory-augmented approaches (e.g., summarization, structured memory, MemGPT-style management), so it is unclear how far current techniques fall short or what a practitioner should do.

The setting is quite artificial: oracle perception/motor skills, text-only observations, a single simulator, and only 12 scenes. The paper acknowledges these limitations but they substantially limit the significance of conclusions about 'real-world personalized assistance.'

Novelty is moderate: personalization in embodied agents (TidyBot, personalized navigation) and episodic-memory evaluations for LLMs already exist; the contribution is a recombination (two-stage memory benchmark on top of PartNR/Habitat) rather than a new capability, method, or insight with strong external validity.
There is no stated commitment to releasing code, dataset, or prompts as an artifact beyond the appendix; reproducibility of the LLM-generated dataset construction pipeline is therefore questionable.

Several presentation issues: Table 3's 'Baseline' rows are under-explained; footnotes for D.5 are duplicated/mislabeled; some claims (e.g., 'highly susceptible to irrelevant memories') are drawn from the patched-retrieval setup described above.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: moving embodied agent evaluation beyond single-turn instruction-following toward personalized assistance grounded in episodic memory, which is an underexplored and relevant direction.

The two-stage Memory Acquisition / Memory Utilization design is a clean and sensible experimental construct that isolates instruction-grounding capability from task-execution capability by holding scene and goal representation fixed, and the validation experiment (Figure 3) supports that utilization-stage instructions are indeed uninterpretable without memory.

Reasonably comprehensive evaluation across six LLMs spanning proprietary and open-source families, with informative metrics (PC, SR, planning cycles, sim steps) and several analyses (knowledge-type breakdown, top-k memory analysis, memory-quality comparison, error taxonomy) that yield interpretable insights, e.g., user patterns are harder than object semantics and irrelevant memories act as distractors.
Discussion experiments (trajectory vs. instruction-only memory; ambiguous indirect references) add analytical value beyond the main table and point toward concrete future directions.
Good reproducibility support: dataset statistics, skill libraries, retrieval implementation, LLM settings, and full prompts are provided in appendices; licenses and societal impact are addressed.
weaknesses: Circularity in data generation and quality control: GPT-4o is used to generate personalized knowledge/instructions, to caption objects, to filter episodes (episodes where GPT-4o failed five attempts were removed), and to produce gold memories. This biases the benchmark toward GPT-4o's distribution and may filter out exactly the hard-but-valid cases, weakening claims about cross-model comparisons.

The evaluation stack is highly oracle-based: ground-truth scene graphs, oracle perception and motor skills, text-only captions instead of visual perception, and a top-5 retrieval setup in which the correct memory is forcibly included if not retrieved. This makes results about 'memory utilization' largely about in-context recall, not end-to-end embodied personalization, limiting ecological validity.

Findings are somewhat expected (performance drops when more memories must be consulted; distractors hurt; small models are worse). The paper is purely diagnostic with no baseline method, adaptation technique, or improvement attempt to demonstrate the benchmark's usefulness in driving progress.

Small sample sizes for key claims: only 36 joint-memory episodes (12 per pair type), making ∆SR values such as 8.3→5.6 or Llama-3.1-70b's -83.4 statistically fragile; no variance estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported for the main comparisons.

Single simulator, single agent architecture (ReAct-style hierarchical planner), and 12 scenes raise questions about generality; the confound that utilization instructions are shorter and stylistically different from acquisition instructions is only partially controlled by the validation experiment.

Some presentation issues: apparent copyediting errors (e.g., 'a white shoe' vs. stated target in the hallucination example; inconsistent Appendix references), and the justification for excluding 31 zero-success episodes relies on GPT-4o failure, which conflates task infeasibility with model difficulty.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: personalized assistance via memory utilization in embodied agents is a timely and underexplored direction, and the paper decomposes it into two well-defined dimensions (object semantics vs. user patterns) that map onto distinct reasoning challenges.

The two-stage evaluation design (memory acquisition vs. memory utilization with identical scenes/goals but varying instructions) is a clever and clean way to isolate memory utilization as the measured factor, with ΔSR/ΔPC providing an interpretable quantification.

Solid benchmark construction practice: built on PartNR/Habitat 3.0, distractor objects to prevent memory-free shortcuts, systematic filtering with explicit criteria, GPT-4o feasibility testing, and inter-rater reliability analysis (Krippendorff's alpha reported per criterion).

Comprehensive experiments: six LLMs across families/sizes, top-k analysis revealing information overload, joint-memory coordination failures, memory format simplification ablations, retrieval strategy analysis, memory quality/noise robustness analysis, 3-joint-memory and ambiguous-instruction extensions, and a human baseline validating task solvability.

Qualitative error taxonomy (Figure 5) is informative, e.g., identifying that agents default to parametric commonsense over non-parametric personalized knowledge—a useful insight for future memory design.
The finding that episodic memory provides both personalized knowledge and in-context learning benefits (summarization hurts smaller models) is a non-obvious, actionable insight.
Good reproducibility posture: anonymous code release, extensive appendices with schemas, algorithms, and full prompts, plus explicit LLM-usage and ethics statements.
weaknesses: Missing comparisons with existing memory architectures: the paper critiques current memory usage but does not evaluate baselines such as MemGPT, MemoryBank, A-Mem, Embodied-RAG, or Reflexion-style memory systems on MEMENTO. Claims that 'current memory architectures' fail are thus supported only by the authors' own naive retrieval setup, weakening the external validity of RQ1/RQ2 conclusions.

The proposed hierarchical knowledge-graph user-profile memory is relatively incremental (a structured profile over KG-style knowledge, in the spirit of MemoryBank/A-Mem/Comet-like graphs), and its evaluation has confounds: the profile memory is retrieved without gold-memory guarantees while episodic memory in the same experiment is supplied with gold memory (Appendix D.3.2), and the profile module itself is built from gold-quality personalized knowledge. The comparison therefore does not isolate the module's contribution under realistic, noisy conditions.

Several experiments use small samples: the memory-format simplification study uses only 30 episodes across 3 scenes, the joint-memory set has only 36 episodes, the human baseline has 4 participants and 20 tasks, and ambiguous/generalization studies use 30-41 tasks. Statistical significance is not reported for any comparisons, and differences like Figure 8's gains could be within noise.

Reliance on guaranteed gold-memory inclusion in the main evaluation (retrieval candidates are randomly replaced to always include gold memories) makes the headline results optimistic relative to realistic retrieval, even though Appendix E.3 partially addresses this.

Some numbers and presentation issues reduce confidence: the extreme Llama-3.1-70b joint-memory drop (ΔSR = -83.4%, SR 8.3%) is not deeply analyzed; Table 9's 'action-type-specific removal' lists '(Place, Place, Navigate)' (typo); occasional grammatical errors ('arere not consistent'); Figure 8's dense annotation makes gains hard to verify against tables; Section 4.2 states 'success rate drop over 20%' for all models but GPT-4o's single-memory ΔSR is -9.9%.

Synthetic, GPT-4o-generated personalized knowledge may not reflect real user knowledge distribution, and oracle perception/motor skills limit ecological validity for embodied deployment—acknowledged by the authors but still constraining the significance of conclusions for real systems.

Scope of memory is narrow: only two memory types (episodic with ReAct traces, plus the proposed profile), a single task family (rearrangement), and no longitudinal/multi-session dynamics (memory accumulation, forgetting, conflict resolution), which are central to personalization claims.

strengths: Clearly motivated and well-scoped research questions (RQ1-RQ3) that structure the paper coherently, moving from evaluation to diagnosis to solution.

The two-stage evaluation design (memory acquisition vs. memory utilization with identical goals but varied instructions) is a sensible and clever way to isolate memory utilization capability from general instruction-following ability.

Substantial evaluation breadth: six LLM agents across model families and sizes, single- vs. joint-memory tasks, breakdowns by personalized knowledge type (object semantics vs. user patterns), top-k retrieval ablations, memory quality/noise robustness analysis, retrieval strategy analysis, and a human baseline study validating task solvability.

Thorough appendix documentation: dataset generation pipeline, quality-control filtering with inter-rater reliability (Krippendorff's alpha), full prompts, algorithm details for the knowledge-graph memory, and an anonymized code release, which supports reproducibility.

The finding that episodic memory provides both personalized knowledge and in-context learning benefits (explaining why summarization hurts smaller models) is an interesting and somewhat non-obvious empirical observation.
Ethics, limitations, privacy, and LLM-usage statements are present and reasonably candid (e.g., acknowledging oracle perception and lack of conversational components).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the two identified bottlenecks (information overload with larger contexts, and coordination failures across multiple memories) largely re-confirm well-known LLM limitations (context-length robustness, multi-example in-context interference). The paper's main empirical surprises are modest.

Potential circularity/confound in dataset construction: instructions and personalized knowledge are generated by GPT-4o, and GPT-4o is also a primary evaluated agent. Filtering episodes where GPT-4o fails five consecutive attempts further biases the benchmark toward GPT-4o-solvable tasks, which may systematically deflate the measured performance gap for GPT-4o relative to other models or inflate everyone's absolute scores; the impact of this choice on the headline findings is not analyzed.

Scale is limited for strong general claims: 201 single-memory episodes and only 36 joint-memory episodes (12 pairs per knowledge-type combination), with small per-condition samples in the memory-design experiments (e.g., 30 episodes for format simplification). Several conclusions rest on differences within confidence intervals that are not reported for the main comparisons.

Unrealistic retrieval setup in the main evaluation: gold memories are always guaranteed within the top-k results. While this isolates memory utilization, it removes retrieval errors entirely from the headline results; the more realistic no-gold-memory setting is relegated to the appendix and shows markedly different behavior (e.g., advanced retrieval strategies hurting performance), which complicates the main conclusions.

The proposed user profile memory is evaluated in a configuration where episodic memory is still supplied with gold memory while profile memory is retrieved without gold, and memory construction/retrieval uses the same LLMs being evaluated; there is limited ablation of the memory module itself (e.g., removing temporal edges, alternative graph granularities), making it hard to attribute gains to the hierarchical design rather than to the cleaner, pre-summarized knowledge format.

Oracle perception and motor skills, combined with a purely text-based setup and a static simulator, limit ecological validity for 'personalized assistance'; the authors acknowledge this, but it further narrows the scope of the contribution.
Some evidence is anecdotal: the qualitative failure taxonomy (Figure 5) is based on sampled cases without quantified frequencies, and the human baseline involves only four participants on 20 tasks.

Claims of 'substantial improvements' from the user-profile memory (Figure 8) are presented without confidence intervals or statistical tests, and per-condition sample sizes are small enough that improvements could be within noise.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and timely gap: evaluating LLM-powered embodied agents' ability to leverage episodic memory for personalized assistance, which prior embodied benchmarks and personalization works have not systematically isolated.

The two-stage evaluation design (memory acquisition vs. memory utilization on identical goals/scene with varied instructions) is a clever and well-motivated way to quantify memory utilization (ΔPC/ΔSR) rather than just overall task performance.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for a benchmark paper: six models across proprietary/open-source families and sizes, breakdowns by knowledge type (object semantics vs. user patterns), top-k memory scaling analysis, joint- and 3-joint-memory tasks, retrieval strategy comparisons, memory noise/corruption robustness tests, and a human baseline study.

Careful dataset construction with quality control: distractor augmentation to prevent memory-free shortcuts, rule-based filtering with explicit criteria, GPT-4o feasibility checks, inter-rater reliability analysis (Krippendorff's alpha), and a human study (100% task solvability) validating that failures are agent-side rather than task-side.

The proposed solution is derived from the analysis rather than added ad hoc: the finding that episodic memory carries both personalized knowledge and in-context learning benefits (explaining why summarization fails, especially in smaller models) directly motivates the hierarchical knowledge-graph user-profile memory, which shows consistent gains on both single- and joint-memory tasks.
Good reproducibility: anonymous code release, extensive appendices with schemas, algorithms, prompts, trajectories, and computing details.
weaknesses: Scale of key experiments is limited: only 438 total episodes, 36 joint-memory tasks, and the memory-format and user-profile experiments in Section 6 use just 30 sampled episodes; several conclusions (e.g., summarization hurting small models, KG memory gains) rest on small sample sizes with no reported confidence intervals or statistical tests.

Dataset is synthetic and generated/filtered with GPT-4o itself, introducing potential circularity (GPT-4o generates personalized knowledge, then is both the primary subject of evaluation and part of the filtering pipeline); inter-rater alphas for Triviality (0.58) and Redundancy (0.57) indicate only moderate annotator agreement on the most subjective filters.

The oracle perception and motor skills setup isolates memory utilization but limits ecological validity; the authors acknowledge this, yet the gap between text-based observations and real visual personalization could be substantial.

Some main findings (information overload from larger contexts, difficulty coordinating multiple sources, defaulting to parametric commonsense) are consistent with known LLM limitations and may be seen as somewhat expected, reducing the novelty of the RQ2 analysis.

The proposed user-profile memory, while effective, is a fairly incremental combination of known techniques (knowledge graphs, LLM-based extraction, hybrid retrieval); its evaluation subset is small and the comparison to alternative structured-memory baselines (e.g., A-Mem, MemoryBank-style designs) is missing.

Minor presentation issues: occasional typos and inconsistencies (e.g., 'Place, Place, Navigate' in Table 9 discussion), Figure 4's truncated y-axis (starting at 40) visually exaggerates differences, and abstract/figure parse quality suggests formatting polish is needed.
Human baseline (4 participants, 20 tasks) is underpowered as an 'upper-bound reference'; more participants and task diversity would strengthen the validation claim.
